items.title: The Hundred Years War lasted 116 years
items.claim: When did the Hundred Years War begin and end?

options.text: 1337 (Edward III claims the French throne) to 1453 (Battle of Castillon) — 116 years, with long truces in between

items.reveal_title: A name invented in the 19th century
items.reveal:
The phrase 'Hundred Years War' was coined by French historians in the 1860s. Contemporaries did not see it as a single conflict but as a series of campaigns separated by long peaces (e.g. the Treaty of Brétigny, 1360).

Major English victories: Crécy (1346), Poitiers (1356), Agincourt (1415). Major French recoveries: Du Guesclin's reconquests under Charles V, and Joan of Arc's relief of Orléans (1429). It ended with the French victory at Castillon in 1453 — three months before Constantinople fell.
items.why: Periodisation is a historical choice, not a fact. A '100 years' war that was actually 116, mostly truce, and named four centuries later is a useful reminder.

items.title: Weimar Germany had a 'golden' decade — but it was built on US loans
items.claim: Why did Weimar's relative stability (1924-1929) collapse?

options.text: The Dawes Plan (1924) restructured reparations with US loans; the Wall Street Crash (October 1929) collapsed lending; Stresemann had died in October 1929; unemployment hit 6 million by 1932
The British naval blockade resumed in 1927

items.reveal:
The Dawes Plan (1924) and Young Plan (1929) refinanced German reparations through US bank loans. Germany used the loans for infrastructure, social housing and reparations payments — a circular flow.

Gustav Stresemann's diplomacy (Locarno 1925, German League membership 1926) normalised relations with the West. He died on 3 October 1929, three weeks before the Wall Street Crash.

When US loans dried up, German banks failed (Danatbank, July 1931); unemployment soared; the Nazis went from 12 seats (1928) to 230 seats (July 1932), becoming the largest party.
items.why: Weimar's 'collapse' was not inevitable but was structurally vulnerable. The Crash was an external shock that destroyed a recovery dependent on foreign credit — a useful case in how interconnected economies fail.

items.title: Constantinople fell to Ottoman cannons in 1453

options.text: Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II besieged Constantinople from 6 April; massive Hungarian-built cannons breached the Theodosian walls; the city fell on 29 May 1453, ending the 1,123-year Eastern Roman Empire

items.reveal:
Mehmed II, aged 21, had artillery cast by Orban, a Hungarian engineer — including the Basilic, around 8 metres long, firing stone balls of around 270 kg. The walls of Theodosius (built 5th century) had held for a thousand years; gunpowder ended their effectiveness.

Emperor Constantine XI Palaiologos died in the fighting; his body was never identified. Around 7,000 Byzantine and Genoese defenders faced perhaps 80,000-150,000 Ottoman troops.

Mehmed converted Hagia Sophia into a mosque (it remained one until 1934, when Atatürk converted it to a museum; reconverted to a mosque in 2020). The fall pushed Greek scholars and texts west into Italy — fuel for the late Renaissance.
items.why: Military technology can end empires. The fall of Constantinople closes the medieval Mediterranean and marks a conventional boundary between medieval and early modern history.
